analysis.one_liner: Gives uninsured people free emergency insulin and taxes insulin makers for price spikes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action after its committee referrals, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a five-year program giving states, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations federal grants to hand out insulin cards to uninsured and underinsured people with a prescription — a 7-day emergency supply within days, then renewable 90-day supplies. Payments made for a person on a high-deductible plan would count toward that plan's deductible. The program would be paid for entirely by annual fees on insulin manufacturers, and insulin makers would also owe an excise tax of 50% to 100% of the revenue from any price increase above inflation. It would also shorten the exclusive market protection for brand-name biologic drugs from 12 years to 7, opening the door to cheaper copies sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people with an insulin prescription, and people with diabetes enrolled in high-deductible health plans who currently pay full price until a large deductible is met. They would get insulin at no cost at the pharmacy, and program payments would count toward their deductible. States and tribes get grants to run the program.

how_it_helps.text: States, tribes, and tribal organizations would get grants to buy insulin and issue cards: an initial card for roughly a 7-day supply issued within 5 business days, and a renewable card for a roughly 90-day supply issued within 12 business days of applying.
Pharmacies would fill prescriptions for card holders at no charge, with the grantee government paying the pharmacy, and would also help people enroll in other programs that cover insulin.
For people on high-deductible health plans, the amount the program pays the pharmacy would have to count toward the plan deductible, so they would not be paying twice for the same insulin.

The program would be funded by annual fees on insulin manufacturers from 2020 through 2024, sized to each year's program cost and split by each manufacturer's share of insulin sales — no new general-revenue spending.

Insulin makers would owe an excise tax on revenue from price increases above general inflation: 50% of the spike revenue for smaller increases, 75% for 15-20% increases, and 100% above 20%, with an escalating multi-year tax for repeated hikes and an exemption if the manufacturer proves the increase came from input costs.
The exclusive market period for brand-name biologic drugs would drop from 12 years to 7, letting biosimilar competitors — typically far cheaper — enter years earlier.

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers, who would pay the annual fees and the excise taxes; makers of brand-name biologics generally, from the shorter exclusivity; and state and tribal budgets, which must contribute $1 for every $3 in federal grant money. Some fee and tax costs could be passed through into drug prices.

drawbacks.text: Grants require a state or tribe to put up $1 of its own money for every $3 of federal funds, which limits which governments can participate and how large a program they can run.
The whole program sunsets 5 years after enactment, so it is a temporary emergency measure, not a lasting fix for insulin prices.
The program covers only insulin, not the rest of diabetes care, and only reaches people who apply and hold a valid prescription; a denied applicant cannot reapply for a year.

Because manufacturers pay fees and excise taxes tied to the drug, some of those costs could be passed into the price of insulin for everyone else — a real tradeoff of charging the industry rather than general taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people rationing insulin today, free emergency supplies are the most direct help a federal bill could offer, and the fee structure means it is paid for by the companies charging the high prices rather than by general taxpayers. The weaknesses are real: the state matching requirement and 5-year sunset limit reach, it helps only with insulin, and industry costs can be partly passed into prices. It is a targeted emergency measure, not a durable price fix — but as emergency measures go, it is aimed squarely at the people being priced out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then a Health subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up, so it never came to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, with Rep. Dean Phillips joining, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
A week later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, which was the last action of any kind.
No markup, hearing, subcommittee vote, or floor vote ever occurred through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers came out ahead: they kept the 12-year exclusivity period, paid no annual fees, and faced no tax on price spikes, while uninsured and high-deductible-plan patients got no relief. The two committees where the bill sat never had to take a position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers kept pricing power and paid nothing

for.name: Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair: Frank Pallone)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of additional referral (Chair: Richard Neal)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral because of its excise tax and fee provisions, and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. All three cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat, so the bill's support was entirely Democratic, but no Republican ever had to go on record against it.

industries.note: The bill would charge them annual fees equal to the full cost of the assistance program, an excise tax of 50-100% of revenue from price increases above inflation, and cut their exclusive market period to 7 years. Their pricing power is exactly what keeps insulin unaffordable for the uninsured, so their interest in this bill runs against patients.
Shortening biologic exclusivity from 12 to 7 years would let cheaper biosimilars reach the market years earlier across the industry, not just for insulin.
They would be paid by grantee governments for every insulin prescription filled for a card holder, adding guaranteed reimbursement volume.

They would have to count program payments toward members' deductibles, which helps patients reach coverage sooner but means the plan starts paying earlier — shifting some insulin costs from the patient to the plan and, in time, premiums.
